case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the President may remove a Federal Trade Commission Commissioner at will notwithstanding the FTC Act’s for-cause removal protection, or whether Humphrey’s Executor remains controlling and constitutionally valid.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution Article II (executive power and Take Care duty) and the Federal Trade Commission Act’s provision limiting removal of FTC Commissioners to removal for cause (e.g., inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (the President and Executive Branch) argue that Article II requires meaningful presidential control over officers exercising executive power, so statutory tenure protections that prevent at-will removal of principal officers are unconstitutional as applied to modern agencies like the FTC. They contend the FTC has evolved since 1935 into a powerful enforcer with significant executive authority, making Humphrey’s Executor either distinguishable, outdated, or wrongly decided; therefore the President’s removal of Commissioner Slaughter should be upheld and the injunction/declaratory relief set aside.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Commissioner Slaughter and aligned parties) argue the removal was plainly unlawful under the FTC Act and squarely controlled by Humphrey’s Executor, which upheld for-cause limits for FTC Commissioners. They maintain the FTC is the paradigmatic independent multimember commission that Humphrey’s Executor and subsequent cases protect; lower courts and a “chorus” of decisions have repeatedly rejected the same Article II arguments. Accordingly, the removal was without legal effect, and judicial relief (including declaratory and injunctive relief) is proper to restore the statutory limits Congress imposed.
key_precedents: Trump v. Wilcox (stay issued), 145 S. Ct. 1415 (May 22, 2025) (as referenced in the materials)
Glenn v. Thomas Fortune Fay, 222 F. Supp. 3d 31 (D.D.C. 2016) (quoted in the district court materials)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch make the most powerful Article II point: the FTC today wields substantial coercive enforcement authority, and for-cause tenure can dilute presidential accountability in precisely the settings where control matters most. But that argument cannot be reconciled with the fact that Humphrey’s Executor upheld this exact for-cause restriction for this exact Commission, and Seila Law treated Humphrey’s as a continuing (though cabined) exception rather than an invitation to revisit the FTC’s status through an evolving “as-applied” functional gloss. As Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, to sustain the at-will removal here we would effectively overrule Humphrey’s in its core application without confronting stare decisis openly, and I am not prepared to do that in this posture. Any reconsideration of Humphrey’s should be direct and explicit; under controlling precedent and the statute’s clear terms, the removal was unlawful.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Roberts rely most heavily on stare decisis and the asserted categorical “Humphrey’s Executor exception” for multimember commissions, but that framing begs the antecedent Article II question: whether officers exercising substantial executive power may be insulated from meaningful presidential control. The founding-era evidence—especially the Decision of 1789—reflects the understanding that the President must be able to remove those who execute the laws to remain accountable, and the FTC’s investigative and enforcement authority is executive in the core sense. While the FTC Act on its face imposes a for-cause limit, applying that limit here prevents the President from supervising principal officers who execute federal law, and Humphrey’s Executor’s “quasi-legislative/quasi-judicial” taxonomy cannot be squared with Article II’s vesting of the executive power in a single President. To the extent Humphrey’s is read to uphold tenure protection for principal officers wielding executive power beyond presidential control, it should not govern this case.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan are right that Humphrey’s Executor is formally on-point and that Seila Law described it as an extant exception, but their stare decisis framing assumes that Humphrey’s necessarily controls even when the agency’s day-to-day work is now predominantly investigative and coercive enforcement—core executive power where Article II supervision is most constitutionally salient. I think we can, consistent with Seila Law and Collins, treat this as an as-applied separation-of-powers problem: whatever insulation Humphrey’s may have approved for genuinely adjudicatory functions cannot constitutionally extend to executive enforcement discretion insulated from at-will removal. Justice Kavanaugh’s concern that this “effectively overrules” Humphrey’s has force, but an as-applied holding can be limited to the Commission’s exercise of executive enforcement authority without repudiating all tenure protection for all independent commissions. On remedy, I agree with Collins that even if the removal restriction is unconstitutional as applied, the petitioner must still show causation for relief rather than receiving automatic vacatur.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is that the modern FTC exercises substantial enforcement authority, and so insulating Commissioners may seem to place core executive functions beyond presidential control. But that argument asks us to treat Seila Law and Collins as if they silently displaced Humphrey’s Executor in its paradigmatic application—this very Commission, with this very for-cause standard—which Seila Law expressly declined to do. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, sustaining at-will removal here would not be a modest application of recent precedent; it would effectively overrule Humphrey’s (and the settled historical tradition it reflects) under the guise of an “as-applied” update. Respect for Congress’s long-used design for multimember independent commissions, and for stare decisis in this on-point setting, requires enforcing the statute’s for-cause limitation and holding the attempted at-will removal unlawful.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the most serious point: the FTC’s present-day enforcement authority is quintessentially executive, and for-cause tenure arguably weakens presidential accountability. But that is not a narrowing distinction from our law; it is precisely the kind of argument Humphrey’s Executor rejected in upholding this Commission with this very “inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance” standard, and Seila Law treated Humphrey’s as a continuing, historically grounded carveout rather than an invitation to invalidate the FTC through an evolving, “as-applied” functional gloss. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, sustaining at-will removal here would effectively overrule Humphrey’s in its paradigmatic application while disclaiming that step, without the stare decisis analysis such a move demands. Under Morrison’s functional inquiry, the President is not “completely stripped” of removal authority and Congress plays no Myers/Bowsher role in removal, so the attempted at-will removal remains unlawful on existing precedent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan are right that Humphrey’s Executor involved this Commission and that Seila Law described it as an extant exception, but that only sharpens the problem: the FTC today exercises quintessential executive power—investigating, prosecuting, and coercively enforcing—and insulating principal officers who wield that power fractures Article II’s chain of dependence in the very setting where democratic accountability must operate. As Justice Thomas stresses, the constitutional injury is present when executive power is exercised by officers the President cannot meaningfully control; we should not convert that structural defect into a remedial “science fiction” inquiry about whether the President would have removed the officer absent the unlawful restriction. If Humphrey’s is understood to bless for-cause tenure for principal executive officers regardless of their enforcement authority, then it supplies no coherent limiting principle consistent with Seila Law, Free Enterprise Fund, and Bowsher, and we should not extend it to sustain coercive executive action unmoored from presidential supervision. Stare decisis matters, but it cannot require us to perpetuate a framework that (as applied to modern executive enforcement) contradicts the Constitution’s allocation of executive power to a single, accountable President.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right to emphasize the Article II accountability problem posed by insulating officials who wield substantial executive enforcement authority; on first principles, the FTC sits at the outer edge of permissible independence. But as the Chief Justice notes, this case involves the paradigmatic Humphrey’s Executor setting—the FTC itself—and Congress also spoke with the requisite clarity by authorizing removal only for “inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance,” which displaces any at-will default absent a constitutional holding. Justice Alito’s proposed “as-applied” path still functions as an implicit overruling of Humphrey’s core application without the forthright stare decisis analysis that step would require. If the Court is to reconsider Humphrey’s, it should do so explicitly in a case framed and briefed for that purpose; under current law, the at-will removal was unlawful.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the most serious point: the FTC’s prosecutorial and enforcement discretion looks like core executive power, and for-cause tenure weakens the President’s supervisory chain in a way that sits uneasily with Article II. But under the FTC Act’s ordinary meaning, the removal restriction applies, and the decisive obstacle—emphasized by the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh—is that Humphrey’s Executor upheld this very for-cause protection for this very Commission; treating the FTC’s modern portfolio as an “as-applied” distinction would effectively overrule Humphrey’s in its paradigmatic application while purporting not to. Seila Law and Collins do not supply a narrow, precedent-grounded principle for invalidating Humphrey’s as applied to the FTC without doing stare decisis work openly. Under Youngstown’s framework and longstanding congressional practice structuring independent commissions, I would hold the at-will removal unlawful and leave any reconsideration of Humphrey’s for a case that squarely presents whether to overrule it.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch present the hardest point: that the FTC’s contemporary investigative and enforcement work looks like quintessential executive power and that for-cause tenure dilutes presidential accountability. But that argument depends on reframing the question into an implied, exclusive presidential removal authority drawn largely from constitutional silence, and then using an “as-applied” label to accomplish what Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh correctly identify as an unacknowledged overruling of Humphrey’s Executor in its core setting—the FTC under this very for-cause standard. Properly framed, the case asks whether Congress’s generally applicable tenure condition on an office it created unlawfully “criminalizes” or eliminates a presidential power; it does not, it constrains only the manner of removal while leaving removal authority intact, as Justice Kagan notes. If the Court is to discard Humphrey’s, it should do so forthrightly with a stare decisis analysis, not indirectly by reclassifying the agency’s functions to evade controlling precedent.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article II removal authority is the rule, and restrictions are permissible only within tightly cabined, historically grounded exceptions; the FTC Act’s for-cause limit falls within the one removal framework this Court has repeatedly treated as a recognized exception—Humphrey’s Executor’s approval of a multimember expert commission. Although the FTC today exercises significant enforcement authority, sustaining at-will removal here would not merely apply existing doctrine but would require extending Seila Law and Collins beyond their “new situation[s]” (single-director or other distinct structures) to overrule or effectively discard Humphrey’s Executor in its core application. Given our approach to stare decisis in separation-of-powers cases and the absence of a narrower structural ground (e.g., insulation by a removable superior) that would resolve this dispute without confronting Humphrey’s Executor head-on, the removal must be treated as unlawful under the governing statute as presently construed. Any change to that settled exception is for the Court to make explicitly, and on this record the President’s asserted need for direct at-will control does not justify rewriting the long-accepted rule for this specific kind of commission.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article II vests the executive power in a single President, and founding-era practice—especially the Decision of 1789—reflects the understanding that the President must be able to remove those who execute the laws in order to remain politically accountable for their administration. The FTC today exercises substantial executive power through investigations, enforcement actions, and prosecutorial discretion, yet the FTC Act’s for-cause tenure protection would allow a principal officer to continue executing federal law against the President’s judgment, placing core executive functions beyond presidential control. Although the statute on its face purports to limit removal to enumerated causes, applying that restriction here is unconstitutional because it prevents meaningful presidential supervision of an executive officer, contrary to Article II’s structure. To the extent Humphrey’s Executor upholds such insulation for officers wielding executive power, it is inconsistent with Article II and should not control this case.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FTC Act’s for-cause limitation (“inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance”) is the same kind of substantial constraint on presidential supervision that Seila Law held unconstitutional when applied to an agency exercising significant executive power, and Collins confirms that such a defect is a separation-of-powers violation even if the remedy turns on causation. Whatever Humphrey’s Executor said about the FTC in 1935, today’s FTC engages in quintessential executive functions—investigations, enforcement actions, and administrative adjudications producing binding orders—so extending Humphrey’s Executor to uphold tenure protection for principal officers wielding that much executive authority would be, at minimum, an extension this Court has repeatedly declined to make. The FTC is not a purely adjudicatory body in the Wiener sense; its enforcement and policymaking roles place it on the executive side of the line, making modern Article II removal precedent more applicable than the older characterization of the Commission as “quasi-legislative” or “quasi-judicial.” Accordingly, I would vote to permit at-will removal as a matter of constitutional structure, while recognizing under Collins that any ultimate relief may still require a showing that the unconstitutional restriction actually caused compensable harm in the challenged decisionmaking chain.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Congress was not silent on removal here: the FTC Act affirmatively provides for-cause protection for Commissioners, reflecting a long historical tradition of Congress insulating certain multimember expert bodies to secure independence. This case fits squarely within the established Humphrey’s Executor/Wiener line approving such protections for bipartisan multimember commissions, and it would require extending (or effectively overruling) that precedent to allow at-will removal. Seila Law, by its own terms, was limited and does not mechanically control because the question is not merely “executive power” in the abstract but whether this structure is the kind of novel, single-Director arrangement with concentrated coercive authority that Seila Law addressed; the FTC’s classic commission form is the paradigm Humphrey’s upheld. Proper respect for Congress’s chosen design therefore requires enforcing the statute’s for-cause limit and treating the attempted at-will removal as unlawful.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Applying our longstanding precedent, the answer is clear: Humphrey’s Executor upheld the FTC Act’s for-cause removal protection for FTC Commissioners, and nothing in this case presents the kind of congressional “participation in the removal” condemned in Myers and Bowsher. Under Humphrey’s and Morrison’s functional inquiry, the President is not “completely stripped” of removal power—he may remove an FTC Commissioner for “inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office”—and that single-layer protection does not by itself “unduly trammel[] on executive authority.” Petitioners’ as-applied argument based on the FTC’s modern enforcement profile asks us to override rather than apply controlling precedent governing precisely this agency’s tenure structure; stare decisis in separation-of-powers cases counsels adherence absent a showing that the statutory limit materially disables the President from carrying out Article II duties. Because the removal here was at-will and contrary to the statute’s for-cause standard, it was unlawful and judicial relief restoring the statutory scheme is proper.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FTC today wields core executive power—investigating, prosecuting, and enforcing federal law—yet the FTC Act forbids the President from removing a Commissioner except for cause, breaking the Article II “chain of dependence” that ensures executive power remains accountable to the people through the President. Under this Court’s separation-of-powers precedents, insulating principal officers who exercise substantial executive authority from at-will presidential control inflicts a here-and-now constitutional injury by subjecting regulated parties to executive action not ultimately controllable by a politically accountable President, without requiring any “science fiction” inquiry into whether the President would have removed the officer absent the restriction. Whatever Humphrey’s Executor said about “quasi-legislative” or “quasi-judicial” functions, that taxonomy cannot justify modern removal insulation for an agency that exercises sweeping enforcement discretion and rulemaking with real-world coercive effect. The FTC Act’s for-cause provision is therefore unconstitutional as applied here, and the President’s removal should be upheld.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FTC Act contains the kind of “very clear and explicit” for-cause language (“inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office”) that, as a statutory matter, displaces the Article II default presumption of at-will removability. On the constitutional question, however strong the Article II accountability concerns may be for a powerful modern FTC that performs substantial executive enforcement, this Court’s precedent has long treated the FTC as the paradigmatic multimember independent commission whose commissioners may be protected by for-cause tenure. Unless and until the Court squarely overrules Humphrey’s Executor, lower courts and this Court are bound to apply it, and the President’s removal concededly not for cause was unlawful under the statute as construed by controlling precedent. The clear-statement canon therefore cuts against the Government’s statutory argument, and stare decisis—given an on-point decision upholding this precise removal limitation—requires affirmance here absent an explicit overruling.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FTC Act’s ordinary meaning squarely provides for-cause removal protection for FTC Commissioners, so the statute applies to the President’s attempted at-will removal here. The remaining question is constitutional: whether applying that protection intrudes on the President’s core Article II supervision-and-removal authority. Under this Court’s separation-of-powers precedents, Seila Law reaffirmed that Humphrey’s Executor remains a recognized exception for multimember commissions, and the FTC fits that paradigm more closely than the novel single-director structure invalidated there; whatever the FTC’s modern enforcement tools, the Court has not overruled Humphrey’s, and I would not treat this case as the vehicle to do so in the absence of a clear doctrinal basis to distinguish it. Applying Youngstown’s framework, Congress’s decision to structure a bipartisan, multimember commission with for-cause tenure falls in an area where Congress has historically legislated and where existing precedent permits some insulation, so I would hold the removal unlawful and leave any broader reconsideration of Humphrey’s to the Court directly and explicitly.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The precise question presented is narrow: whether the President may disregard the FTC Act’s for-cause removal restriction as to an FTC Commissioner, and on that question Humphrey’s Executor squarely upheld the constitutionality of that very statutory protection for this very Commission. Petitioners’ request to recast the case into a broad pronouncement that Article II confers an implied, exclusive presidential removal power over all principal officers relies on “indefinite constitutional language” where the text is silent on at-will removal, and it asks the Court to decide far more than is necessary to resolve this dispute. Properly framed, the FTC Act is not a law that “criminalizes” or negates a presidential power; it is a generally applicable structural constraint Congress imposed on an office Congress created, regulating the manner of removal while leaving the President’s supervisory tools and the Commission’s existence intact. Consistent with separation-of-powers accountability principles and ordinary judicial review, the President’s at-will removal was unlawful under the statute, and the appropriate remedy is to enforce Congress’s for-cause limit absent a compelling basis to overrule controlling precedent.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the President may remove a sitting Federal Trade Commission Commissioner at will notwithstanding statutory for-cause removal protections and the Supreme Court’s decision in Humphrey’s Executor.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution Article II (executive power and Take Care Clause) as applied to the President’s removal authority; and the Federal Trade Commission Act’s for-cause removal restriction for FTC Commissioners (as understood through Humphrey’s Executor).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (President Trump and the United States) argue that insulating FTC Commissioners from at-will removal violates Article II because FTC Commissioners exercise substantial executive power, and that Humphrey’s Executor should be narrowed, distinguished, or overruled—especially given the modern FTC’s expanded authority—so that the President must be able to remove Commissioners to ensure democratic accountability and faithful execution of the laws.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Commissioner Slaughter and allied parties) argue that the FTC Act’s for-cause removal protection is valid and directly controlled by Humphrey’s Executor, that Slaughter’s removal was therefore unlawful and without legal effect, and that longstanding precedent and repeated lower-court rejections of similar challenges confirm that independent, multimember expert commissions may be protected from at-will presidential removal.
key_precedents: Trump v. Wilcox (stay issued), 145 S. Ct. 1415 (May 22, 2025) (referenced as involving NLRB/MSPB removals)
Glenn v. Thomas Fortune Fay, 222 F. Supp. 3d 31 (D.D.C. 2016) (quoted)
Harris, 2025 WL 980278 (D.C. Cir. 2025) (referenced concurrences/dissent discussing Humphrey’s Executor/Wiener)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett are right that Humphrey’s Executor upheld this very for-cause provision for this very Commission, and that Seila Law and Collins distinguished rather than overruled it; that is the strongest stare decisis point. But we should treat Humphrey’s as a narrow, historically bounded exception tied to the character of the office as then understood, and the modern FTC’s substantial investigative and enforcement authority makes this a materially different application—one that more directly implicates Article II’s baseline of presidential supervision and accountability emphasized since the Decision of 1789. I do not think we can convert Humphrey’s into a roving license for insulating principal officers exercising significant executive power merely because the agency is multimember and nominally “independent.” The proper remedy is severance of the for-cause restriction, allowing the Commission to function independently with at-will removal while preserving the remainder of the statutory scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is stare decisis: Humphrey’s Executor upheld this very for-cause restriction for this very Commission, and our later cases have distinguished rather than overruled it. But that only underscores the problem: Humphrey’s rests on the “quasi-legislative”/“quasi-judicial” taxonomy that cannot be reconciled with Article II’s Vesting Clause and the founding-era understanding—reflected in the Decision of 1789—that presidential removal is a core incident of the executive power necessary for accountability. As Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the FTC’s investigation and enforcement authority is quintessentially executive, and insulating principal officers wielding that power from at-will removal fractures the unitary executive and impairs the President’s Take Care duty. Where precedent conflicts with the Constitution’s structure, we should at minimum narrow Humphrey’s to its facts and invalidate the removal restriction as applied to officers exercising substantial executive power, with severability preserving the Commission’s continued operation under at-will removal.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is that Humphrey’s Executor upheld this very statute for this very Commission, and that Seila Law and Collins expressly distinguished rather than overruled it—so narrowing Humphrey’s risks overruling-by-relabeling. But that objection assumes Humphrey’s functional premises remain accurate; as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch stress, the modern FTC exercises substantial coercive executive power through investigation and enforcement, and insulating principal officers wielding that power from at-will removal is hard to reconcile with our Article II accountability analysis in Seila Law. Treating Humphrey’s as an unbounded safe harbor would constitutionalize an outdated “quasi-judicial/quasi-legislative” description and extend an exception beyond its justification, whereas the sounder course is to sever the for-cause restriction while leaving Collins’s causation inquiry to govern any retrospective remedy. Stare decisis has force, but it does not require us to freeze a functional misdescription into a permanent constitutional rule when the agency’s present-day authority triggers the structural concern our recent precedents recognize.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point on the other side: that the modern FTC’s investigative and enforcement tools look “more executive” and therefore demand tighter presidential supervision as a matter of Article II accountability. But that functional recharacterization cannot do the work they ask without effectively overruling Humphrey’s Executor “by application,” even though Seila Law and Collins repeatedly distinguished Humphrey’s rather than displacing it—and this case involves the same agency and the same single-layer for-cause provision Humphrey’s upheld. Nor does their structural-injury framing answer the key doctrinal fact Justice Kagan emphasizes: Congress did not seize removal for itself; it set a for-cause standard while leaving the removal decision with the President, a design our precedents have long treated as permissible for multimember commissions. If the Court is to narrow or overrule Humphrey’s because the FTC has become too “executive,” it must confront stare decisis and reliance candidly rather than recasting the agency’s functions as a backdoor to the same result.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point—that the modern FTC’s enforcement activity is “predominantly executive” and thus outside Humphrey’s—ultimately asks us to do by characterization what Seila Law and Collins declined to do by holding: treat Humphrey’s as effectively obsolete for the very Commission and for-cause clause it upheld. That approach supplies no administrable principle for when an agency becomes “too executive” to fall within Humphrey’s, and it would amount to overruling-by-application without the stare decisis analysis our institutional role demands, as Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize. Under Morrison’s functional inquiry, this single-layer for-cause protection—leaving removal with the President for inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance—does not unduly trammel Article II authority in the way dual insulation did in Free Enterprise Fund. If the Court wishes to narrow or overrule Humphrey’s, it should confront reliance and precedent directly rather than re-labeling the FTC’s mix of functions to reach the same destination.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh make the best case on stare decisis: Humphrey’s Executor did uphold this very FTC provision, and Seila Law and Collins distinguished rather than overruled it. But that precedent rested on a “quasi-legislative/quasi-judicial” description that cannot bear the constitutional weight placed on it when today’s FTC wields substantial coercive executive power through investigation, enforcement discretion, and binding orders—authority our cases treat as requiring meaningful presidential supervision. As the Chief Justice stresses, the constitutional harm is structural and present: a broken chain of dependence is not cured by a remedial inquiry into whether a particular President would have fired a particular Commissioner. The least disruptive and most faithful path is to read Humphrey’s narrowly, hold the for-cause restriction unconstitutional as applied to these executive functions, and sever it to restore Article II accountability while preserving the Commission.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch make the strongest Article II case that the modern FTC’s enforcement activity looks quintessentially executive and that at-will removal promotes presidential supervision and accountability. But this case involves an express, clear for-cause provision in the FTC Act, and Humphrey’s Executor upheld that very restriction for this very Commission; Seila Law and Collins repeatedly distinguished Humphrey’s rather than displacing it. Narrowing Humphrey’s “as applied” on the ground that the FTC has become “more executive” would operate as overruling-by-application without the stare decisis analysis and administrable limiting principle Justice Kagan identifies. Given the clear statutory text and directly controlling precedent, I would enforce the for-cause restriction here and leave any reconsideration of Humphrey’s for a case that squarely presents that question.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch that the modern FTC exercises substantial coercive enforcement authority, and that insulation of principal officers can create a structural Article II concern. But at the threshold, the statute’s ordinary meaning imposes a for-cause limit, and Humphrey’s Executor upheld that very limit for this very Commission; Seila Law and Collins repeatedly distinguished Humphrey’s rather than displacing it, so an “as-applied” narrowing based on updated functional characterizations would operate as overruling without the stare decisis analysis that step requires. On the constitutional question, a single layer of for-cause protection for a multimember commission does not, without more (e.g., dual insulation or a single director), present the kind of clear “danger of intrusion” into core presidential authority that would justify disregarding the statute and precedent. If the Court believes Humphrey’s is wrong or unworkable given modern agency practice, it should say so candidly and undertake the reliance and doctrinal analysis that overruling entails, rather than re-labeling the FTC’s functions to reach the same result.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s point that founding-era practice may suggest an at-will removal “baseline,” and that the modern FTC’s enforcement work looks more executive than Humphrey’s Executor’s functional description contemplated. But that broad structural framing elides the question actually presented here: whether we may disregard Congress’s express, single-layer for-cause standard for this multimember Commission when Humphrey’s upheld this very provision for this very agency, and Seila Law and Collins conspicuously distinguished rather than displaced it. Treating Humphrey’s as effectively obsolete “as applied” because the FTC’s mix of functions has evolved would operate as overruling-by-relabeling without the stare decisis analysis Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett properly demand. Absent a genuinely new structural feature (e.g., a single director or dual insulation), I would apply Humphrey’s and hold the President’s attempted at-will removal ineffective under the FTC Act.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article II’s baseline rule, grounded in text, first principles, and historical practice since 1789, is that the President must be able to remove executive officers to ensure accountability for the faithful execution of the laws. The modern FTC exercises substantial executive power—investigating, enforcing, and initiating administrative proceedings that carry significant coercive effect—so insulating Commissioners from at-will removal prevents meaningful presidential control over officials wielding executive authority. Humphrey’s Executor is best read as a narrow, historically bounded exception tied to the Commission’s described “quasi-legislative” and “quasi-judicial” character, and we should not extend that exception to a new situation where the agency’s core functions and practical power are predominantly executive. Because the constitutional defect lies in the for-cause restriction rather than the existence of the FTC, that removal protection is severable and the FTC can function independently with Commissioners removable at will, with no clear indication Congress would have preferred no Commission at all to one accountable to the President.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article II vests the executive power in a single President, and the founding-era understanding—confirmed by the Decision of 1789—treated presidential removal of executive officers as a core incident of that power necessary to preserve accountability for faithful execution of the laws. FTC Commissioners exercise substantial executive power through investigation, prosecution, and enforcement of federal law, and insulating them by a for-cause removal restriction allows them to execute the laws beyond the President’s control in derogation of the Take Care duty. The constitutional defect is not that the FTC is labeled “independent,” but that otherwise executive officers are shielded from at-will removal in a way that fractures the unitary executive and dilutes political accountability. To the extent Humphrey’s Executor authorizes such insulation for officers wielding executive power, it is inconsistent with Article II’s structure and should be narrowed or overruled as applied here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Assuming Article III standing is satisfied because the President’s asserted inability to remove a sitting Commissioner is a concrete institutional injury traceable to the FTC Act’s for-cause restriction and redressable by a declaration that the restriction is unenforceable, the merits turn on separation of powers. The modern FTC exercises substantial executive power through investigations and enforcement actions, and its Commissioners are principal officers; insulating them from at-will removal materially diminishes the President’s Article II authority to supervise execution of the laws. Although Humphrey’s Executor upheld for-cause protection for the FTC in 1935, Seila Law’s analysis is all but dispositive to the extent it rejects insulation of officers wielding significant executive power, and Humphrey’s should be narrowed (and, if necessary, overruled) to the extent it cannot be reconciled with that framework for today’s FTC. Finally, any remedy must still turn on causation—i.e., whether the for-cause restriction actually prevented removal or otherwise altered executive action—but that remedial inquiry does not salvage the restriction’s constitutionality.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Congress here affirmatively provided a simple for-cause removal protection for FTC Commissioners, so the Myers at-will default does not control. Under Humphrey’s Executor, that exact statutory design for the FTC is constitutional, and the Court’s more recent decisions (Free Enterprise Fund, Seila Law, Collins) repeatedly distinguished—rather than overruled—Humphrey’s Executor when addressing different, novel structures (e.g., dual for-cause layers or a single-headed agency). Even if the modern FTC wields substantial authority affecting private parties, it remains a multimember expert commission of principal officers removable by the President for cause, a form of independence this Court has long permitted and that Congress may choose to secure nonpartisan, expert administration. Because the for-cause restriction is valid under controlling precedent, the President’s attempted at-will removal was unlawful and without legal effect.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Humphrey’s Executor is directly controlling: it upheld this very statute’s for-cause removal protection for FTC Commissioners, and nothing in our subsequent cases has overruled it. Read properly, Myers and Bowsher condemn Congress’s own participation in removals; they do not prohibit Congress from merely limiting the President’s removal power through a for-cause standard where the President retains the removal decision. Applying the functional test, a single layer of for-cause protection for a multimember commission does not “unduly trammel[ ] on executive authority” in a way that prevents the President from carrying out Article II duties, especially given the long-settled reliance interests surrounding independent commissions. The government’s argument that the modern FTC’s powers have evolved is a request to narrow or discard precedent, but our separation-of-powers law has treated Humphrey’s as the anchor for this category of agency, and stare decisis counsels adhering to it here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FTC today wields substantial executive power—investigating, prosecuting, adjudicating, and seeking enforcement of binding orders—and the FTC Act’s for-cause tenure protection denies the President effective supervisory control over those executive decisions. That combination breaks the Article II “chain of dependence” by vesting executive power in officers the President cannot hold to account, a present structural injury under our separation-of-powers precedents rather than something courts should test through counterfactual inquiries into whether the President would have removed a Commissioner absent the restriction. Whatever Humphrey’s Executor once said about a “quasi-legislative” or “quasi-judicial” commission, subsequent decisions have emphasized that executive power must remain accountable to a nationally elected President, and the modern FTC’s enforcement and prosecutorial functions underscore the constitutional problem here. The proper course is to recognize the removal restriction as unconstitutional as applied to an agency exercising significant executive authority, allowing at-will removal to restore democratic accountability.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article II’s text and structure generally support a presumption of at-will removability, and I do not infer for-cause protection from silence or statutory labels. But here Congress did not proceed by implication: the FTC Act contains an explicit for-cause removal restriction, and that is precisely the arrangement this Court upheld for the FTC in Humphrey’s Executor. Under principles of stare decisis—especially where Congress has legislated against that settled backdrop—the President may not remove an FTC Commissioner at will unless and until this Court overrules or materially narrows Humphrey’s Executor, which I would not do on these facts. The proper course is to apply Humphrey’s Executor as controlling precedent to the FTC’s multimember structure and express for-cause standard, even if modern Article II cases raise serious constitutional concerns at the margins.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As a threshold matter, the FTC Act’s ordinary meaning plainly provides that Commissioners may be removed only for cause, and that statutory restriction directly covers the President’s attempted at-will removal here. With the statute applicable, the constitutional question is whether enforcing the for-cause limit in these circumstances poses a “danger of intrusion on the authority and functions of the Executive Branch”; under our existing doctrine, Humphrey’s Executor has already answered that question for the FTC as a multimember commission with a mix of quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial functions. While Seila Law and Collins cast doubt on broad insulation for single-director agencies exercising substantial executive power, they expressly distinguished the Humphrey’s Executor category rather than overruling it, and I would adhere to that controlling precedent on an as-applied challenge involving a traditional multimember commission. Because the removal restriction does not, under Humphrey’s Executor, impermissibly trench on a core Article II supervisory/removal power in this established setting, the President may not remove the Commissioner at will.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The precise question presented is not whether the President possesses executive power in the abstract, but whether a generally applicable statutory limit—Congress’s for-cause protection in the FTC Act—unlawfully constrains the manner in which the President may remove an FTC Commissioner. Humphrey’s Executor squarely upheld that very removal restriction for this very multimember Commission, grounding the result in the FTC’s statutory structure (fixed terms, bipartisan composition, and for-cause standard) and its assigned adjudicatory and rulelike functions; deciding this case does not require reframing the question into a broader theory of “core” presidential removal authority untethered to text. Petitioners’ invitation to narrow or overrule Humphrey’s Executor rests largely on implied Article II premises and functional concerns about “accountability,” but those generalized appeals cannot justify disregarding controlling precedent and the specific congressional design that cabins removal only to “inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance.” On this record, the President’s at-will removal of a sitting Commissioner is legally ineffective because it contravenes the FTC Act as authoritatively construed by this Court.
